script.opening: (Upbeat, determined, a little impatient.) "So it's my foot again — the doctor at the walk-in thinks it's another stress fracture. That's the third one this year, which is so annoying. Look, I've got races coming up, so can you just sort it, maybe a boot or whatever, so I can get back to training as fast as possible? I really don't want to lose fitness."

facts.text: "It hurts walking now. It started as just a niggle on long runs and I kept going." Top of the left foot, three weeks. Walk-in centre gave a walking boot and crutches. Previous fractures: right shin (6 months ago), left heel bone (10 months ago).
"I've been building my mileage for the season. I train most days" — about 90 km a week plus gym. Club runner aiming for a half-marathon qualifying time.

"I eat healthily. I'm careful, that's all — you have to be at my level." If asked gently with screening questions: "I don't really want to get into all that. I'm not ill. I just watch what I eat." Cuts carbs, skips meals on rest days, weighs herself daily. If asked kindly and directly: has occasionally made herself sick after a big meal "a couple of times". Lost about 5 kg this year.

"I don't really keep track. Isn't that normal for runners anyway?" Came off the combined pill 18 months ago; periods since then "few and far between" — last one about 5 months ago. Not sexually active at the moment.
"I'm tired, but everyone's tired. I do get stressed about races." Feels cold a lot, dizzy when standing quickly, frequent colds this year. No palpitations or fainting.
No regular medicines; takes a multivitamin. No allergies. No previous eating disorder diagnosis. Mum has osteoporosis? — "No, but my gran broke her hip."
Final-year sports science student, lives in a shared house. Doesn't drink much, non-smoker. Coach "wants me lighter for racing".
"Running is basically everything. If I can't train I don't really know who I am. That's what scares me."

Bright and focused on getting back to running. Becomes guarded if eating is raised bluntly or in a judging way. Opens up a little if the doctor links eating to performance and bone health rather than weight: "So you think I'm not eating enough? … I hadn't thought of it like that." Agrees to a dietitian; hesitant about eating-disorder services: "A dietitian's fine. The other bit… maybe. Not yet." Does not want her coach or parents told: "No, keep it between us for now."

ice.ideas: "Bad luck with my foot — I just need a boot and to get back running."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — running is her identity; she restricts food tightly and is frightened of losing control of her weight and fitness; she doesn't see herself as ill.
ice.expectations: "A quick fix so I can get back to training."

cues: "Third one this year." — invites asking why.
"I'm careful, that's all." — the eating she plays down.
"If I can't train I don't really know who I am." — the fear to acknowledge.

checkpoints.text: Recognises RECURRENT stress fractures (three in a year) in a young female athlete as a RED FLAG for an underlying systemic cause (RED-S) — resisting "just fix the foot"

Understands RED-S (IOC 2023, international: wider than the female athlete triad and affecting men too) (low energy availability ± disordered eating, menstrual dysfunction, impaired bone health, plus mood/immune/performance effects)

Screens EATING and ENERGY availability sensitively and non-judgementally (intake vs training, restriction, weight/body preoccupation, purging — using any tool such as SCOFF only as a prompt, never the sole basis, NICE NG69) recognising disordered eating may be hidden behind performance goals
Takes a MENSTRUAL history — identifies amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea as a key clue and recognises the COMBINED PILL can MASK it — never dismissing lost periods as "just from running"

Arranges a face-to-face examination and investigates appropriately (confirm fracture; FBC, ferritin, vitamin D, TFTs, coeliac; in amenorrhoea a pregnancy test first, then LH/FSH/oestradiol and prolactin; consider DEXA, NICE NG69) and refers MULTIDISCIPLINARY (sports medicine, dietitian, eating-disorder/psychology), advising fuelling and modified training, and knowing the combined pill does not protect bone
Engages a performance-focused patient gently, connects the fractures to under-fuelling in a way she can hear, and explores possible eating disorder/perfectionism without shaming
Frames adequate fuelling and bone health as the route to better performance and staying in her sport, addressing the fear of losing running
Safety-nets and follows up: arranges investigations and referrals, monitors bone/menstrual/eating recovery, and reviews — treating the energy deficiency, not just the fracture

worked.txt: "I’ll absolutely help your foot — but three stress fractures in a year isn’t bad luck, it’s your body telling us something bigger, and if we only treat the bone you’ll be back with a fourth. Can we look at why this keeps happening?"

"In runners, repeated fractures often come down to not taking in enough fuel for the training load — sometimes without realising. Can you talk me through what a normal day’s eating looks like against how much you’re running?"

"Can I ask about your periods — are they regular, or have they stopped or become irregular? … And are you on the pill? Because the pill can hide this. Losing your periods with heavy training isn’t normal — it’s a sign your body’s running low, and it weakens bone. And the pill won’t protect your bones — it just hides the signal."

"Some athletes get very focused on food, weight or ‘eating clean’ — sometimes it tips into restricting. Is any of that part of the picture for you? There’s no judgement here — I ask because it’s common and it really matters for your bones."

"I’d like to see you in person to look at your foot and check your weight, pulse and blood pressure, and do a pregnancy test and some bloods including your iron, vitamin D and hormones, and a bone-density scan given the fractures. And I’d bring in a sports doctor and a dietitian — and, if helpful, someone to support the eating side — so we fix the cause."

"Here’s the key: fuelling properly and getting your periods back isn’t the enemy of performance — it’s how you run faster and stay injury-free in the sport you love. Let’s heal the foot AND sort the bigger picture, together."

f.learning: A single stress fracture can be a training error, but THREE in a year in a young female runner is a red flag for a systemic cause — RELATIVE ENERGY DEFICIENCY IN SPORT (RED-S) — not just a foot to fix, so resist the patient’s "just sort it" framing. RED-S arises from low energy availability (insufficient intake for training expenditure, intentional or not) and — while the IOC 2023 consensus (international) describes REDs as wider than the older female athlete triad, affecting men too — the triad’s core is low energy availability (with or without disordered eating), menstrual dysfunction (amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea from hypothalamic suppression), and impaired bone health (low density causing stress fractures), alongside effects on mood, immunity and performance. Screen eating and energy availability sensitively and non-judgementally (intake versus training volume, restriction, weight/body preoccupation, purging, beliefs about thinness and performance — a tool such as SCOFF only as a prompt, never the sole basis, NICE NG69), recognising disordered eating in athletes is common and often hidden behind "clean eating" or performance goals. Take a menstrual history — amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea is a cardinal sign and major bone-health risk, the combined pill can MASK it by producing withdrawal bleeds, and lost periods in an athlete are never "just from running". Examine face to face (not possible on video; physical risk assessment if eating is restricted, RCPsych MEED CR233) and investigate appropriately (confirm the fracture; FBC, ferritin, vitamin D, TFTs, coeliac; in amenorrhoea a pregnancy test first, then LH, FSH, oestradiol and prolactin; consider DEXA for bone density, NICE NG69) and manage the energy deficiency, not just the bone, with multidisciplinary referral (sports medicine, dietitian, eating-disorder services/psychology), optimised vitamin D/calcium, the knowledge that the combined pill does not protect bone, and modified training with adequate fuelling — the bone will not heal durably without correcting the energy deficit. The hidden agenda is that training/performance and possibly eating/body control are central to her identity, with minimisation, perfectionism or an eating disorder beneath and fear of losing running; engage gently, connect the fractures to under-fuelling, frame fuelling as the route to performance, and bring her toward help without shaming.

knowledge.guideline: IOC consensus statement on REDs 2023 (international) · NICE NG69 (eating disorders, 2017, updated 2020) · RCPsych MEED CR233 (2022)
knowledge.summary: Three stress fractures in a year in a young woman who runs is a systemic warning, not bad luck. Screen for low energy availability, disordered eating and menstrual disturbance, look for low bone density, and treat the cause with a team, not just the bone.

points.h: Recurrent bone stress injury is the red flag
points.t: One stress fracture can follow a jump in training load. Repeated ones point to low energy availability and poor bone health. Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) is wider than the old female athlete triad: it affects men too, and reaches bone, hormones, mood, immunity, heart and performance [1].

points.h: Screen eating by conversation, not a score
points.t: Ask about intake against training, restriction, food rules, weight and shape worries, purging, laxatives and over-exercise. A tool such as SCOFF can prompt the conversation but must not be the only way you decide whether an eating disorder is present [2]. If you suspect one, refer immediately to the community eating-disorder service [2].

points.h: Periods are a vital sign, and the pill can hide them
points.t: Absent or infrequent periods in an athlete are a sign of low energy availability, not a normal effect of running. Withdrawal bleeds on a combined pill mask this, so ask what she takes. Always do a pregnancy test first in amenorrhoea, then LH, FSH, oestradiol, prolactin and TFTs.

points.h: Investigate the bone and the cause
points.t: Confirm the fracture (MRI is the most sensitive test; X-ray is often normal early). Bloods: FBC, ferritin, U and E, bone profile, vitamin D, TFTs, coeliac serology. Consider DXA: NICE NG69 advises DXA earlier than usual when there are recurrent fractures [2]. A fracture at a high-risk site (for example the navicular or the base of the fifth metatarsal) needs an urgent orthopaedic or sports-medicine opinion.

points.h: Check physical risk before assuming she is well
points.t: If eating is significantly restricted, assess medical risk in person: weight and BMI, lying and standing pulse and BP, temperature, the sit-up–squat–stand test and an ECG and electrolytes if indicated [3]. A video call cannot do this.

points.h: Treat the energy deficit, not the fracture alone
points.t: Relative rest from impact, more fuel, and a team: sports and exercise medicine, a sports dietitian, and eating-disorder or psychology input where needed. Correct vitamin D deficiency (dose per BNF). The combined pill is not advised to protect bone in hypothalamic amenorrhoea; if hormone therapy is needed, specialists use transdermal oestradiol with cyclical progesterone [1].

dg.d: Open question; lets her explain the foot and her goal of racing; agrees an agenda that includes “why does this keep happening?”.
Training load, identity as a runner, club or coach pressure, stress about races, mood and sleep.
Face-to-face exam with weight, pulse, BP, temperature; imaging of the foot; pregnancy test, FBC, ferritin, U and E, bone profile, vitamin D, TFTs, coeliac, LH, FSH, oestradiol, prolactin; DXA.
Low energy availability (REDs) versus training error alone; disordered eating; other causes of amenorrhoea (pregnancy, thyroid, prolactin, PCOS); coeliac or vitamin D deficiency.
High-risk fracture site; physical instability from restriction (bradycardia, postural drop, electrolyte disturbance); a significant eating disorder needing immediate referral.
Recurrent bone stress injury, probably from relative energy deficiency in sport, shared in plain language without blame.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Relative rest from impact; team referral (sports medicine, sports dietitian, eating-disorder service if suspected); fuelling framed as the route to performance.
Checks contraception (pill can mask amenorrhoea, and does not protect bone); vitamin D replacement if low; mood and stress.
Face-to-face review this week, results review, named red flags (fainting, palpitations, severe pain, low mood), confidentiality with her club respected.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picks up “I’m careful what I eat”, “isn’t that normal for runners?” and the fear of losing fitness, and explores each.
Idea: bad luck; concern: losing running and the identity attached to it; expectation: a quick fix to keep training.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — running is her identity; she restricts food tightly and is frightened of losing control of her weight and fitness; she doesn't see herself as ill — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Orla, I’m Dr Lee. I’ve seen the walk-in note about your foot. I’m sorry — I can hear how frustrating this is. Tell me what’s happened, and what you’re hoping we can do today.
model.why: Opens with her story and her expectations, not a checklist

model.text: It’s my foot again. They think it’s another stress fracture — third one this year. I’ve got races coming up, so I just need it sorted. A boot or whatever, so I can get back to training fast.

Getting you back running is exactly what I want too. I’ll make sure the foot is properly looked after. But I’d also like to understand why this keeps happening, because three in a year tells me something. Can we cover both today?
model.why: Agrees a shared agenda that includes the systemic question

model.text: I suppose. I just thought it was bad luck.
Talk me through the foot first — where is the pain, and is it there when you walk, or only when you run?
model.why: Focused fracture history to judge severity and site

model.text: It hurts walking now. It started as just a niggle on long runs and I kept going.
Thanks. And what does a normal week of training look like at the moment — has anything changed in the last few months?
model.why: Establishes training load, the other half of the energy balance

model.text: I’ve been building my mileage for the season. I train most days.

That’s a big load. Repeated stress fractures in runners often come down to the body not getting enough fuel for the training — often without anyone meaning it to. Could you walk me through what you’d eat on a typical training day?
model.why: Explains why before asking a sensitive question, so it lands as curiosity not accusation

model.text: I eat healthily. I’m careful, that’s all — you have to be at my level.

Lots of athletes say that. Can I ask a bit more — do you ever skip meals, have rules about what you will or won’t eat, or feel guilty if you eat more than planned? Any making yourself sick or using laxatives? There’s no judgement here; I ask everyone who has bones breaking like this.
model.why: Screens restriction, food rules and compensatory behaviours in a normalised way

model.text: I don’t really want to get into all that. I’m not ill. I just watch what I eat.
That’s fair, and you don’t have to answer everything today. I’ll leave the door open. Can I ask about your periods — are they regular, and are you on any contraception?
model.why: Respects her pace and moves to the key clue: menstrual history and the pill

model.text: I don’t really keep track. Isn’t that normal for runners anyway?

It’s common, but it isn’t normal or harmless — it’s one of the clearest signs the body is running low on energy, and it weakens bone. And if someone is on the combined pill, the monthly bleed can hide the problem completely, so I’ll check exactly what you take.
model.why: Corrects the myth and names the masking effect of the pill

model.text: How are you in yourself — energy, mood, sleep, picking up lots of colds, or feeling your running has stalled even though you train harder?
model.why: Screens the wider effects of low energy availability

model.text: I’m tired, but everyone’s tired. I do get stressed about races.
You’ve said a few times you don’t want to lose fitness. What would it mean for you if you had to step back from running for a while?
model.why: Explores the real concern behind “just sort my foot”

model.text: Running is basically everything. If I can’t train I don’t really know who I am. That’s what scares me.
Thank you for telling me that. It makes complete sense that this feels threatening. My aim is the opposite of taking running away — it’s to stop your body breaking so you can keep doing it for years.
model.why: Validates the fear and reframes the doctor as an ally for her sport

model.text: Here’s what I think is going on. When training uses more energy than food puts back in, the body saves energy by turning down things it sees as optional — periods, hormones, bone repair. That’s called low energy availability, and it’s the commonest reason for repeated stress fractures in runners. It isn’t about willpower or blame.
model.why: Plain-language explanation of REDs linking fractures, periods and fuel

model.text: So you think I’m not eating enough?
I think it’s the most likely explanation, and I’d like to check rather than guess. The upside is real: athletes who fuel properly usually get their periods back, heal better and often run faster.
model.why: Frames fuelling as the route to performance, not a punishment

model.text: I hadn’t thought of it like that.

For the foot: I’d like to see you in person this week to examine it, check your weight, pulse and blood pressure, and arrange the right scan. Until then, please don’t run on it. If it’s in certain higher-risk spots in the foot, it needs a bone specialist quickly.
model.why: Arranges face-to-face assessment, imaging and relative rest; flags high-risk sites

model.text: No running at all? Okay… if it means it heals properly.

Alongside that, some blood tests — a pregnancy test because periods are irregular, blood count, iron, vitamin D, kidney and bone salts, thyroid, coeliac and hormone levels — and a bone-density scan, because three fractures is enough reason to look.
model.why: Pregnancy test first, then a targeted work-up and DXA

model.text: Then I’d like to get you the right team: a sports medicine doctor and a sports dietitian who works with runners. And if food ever feels harder to manage than you’d like, there’s specialist support for that too — your choice when. How does that sound?
model.why: Multidisciplinary referral offered as a choice, keeping the eating-disorder route open without labelling

model.text: A dietitian’s fine. The other bit… maybe. Not yet.

That’s okay. If what we find suggests an eating problem, I’ll talk to you openly before referring, because early help works best. And one question for your club or coach — would you like me to share anything with them? Only if you want me to.
model.why: Honest about the referral threshold; respects adult confidentiality

model.text: No, keep it between us for now.

Of course. Please call us or 111 sooner if the pain becomes severe or constant at rest, you feel faint or dizzy, your heart races or feels irregular, or you notice your mood dropping badly. I’ll see you face to face this week and again when the results are back.
model.why: Specific safety-net, including physical-risk and mood symptoms, with booked follow-up

model.text: Okay. That’s more than I expected, but it makes sense.
Can you tell me in your own words what we’re doing next, so I know I’ve explained it well?
model.why: Teach-back checks understanding

model.text: Rest the foot, come in this week, bloods and a bone scan, see a sports doctor and dietitian. And think about the fuelling thing.
Perfect. You did the right thing getting this looked at properly. Anything else you wanted to ask?
model.why: Closes warmly and shares the floor

social.t: For a competitive athlete, running can be her identity, social world and coping strategy. Leanness culture, coach expectations and race targets can drive under-fuelling; explore them without blame.
“Clean” or “careful” eating in athletes can hide restriction. Many do not see it as a problem, so aim for trust and a door left open rather than a confession today.

legal.t: She is a competent adult. Do not share information with her coach, club or governing body without her consent (GMC Confidentiality, 2017), unless there is a serious risk to life.

legal.h: Capacity and the Mental Health Act
legal.t: Her decisions about training and treatment are hers while she has capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Compulsory treatment only arises in severe, life-threatening eating disorders and is not the issue today.

professional.t: Fracture assessment and eating-disorder physical-risk checks need an in-person review (RCPsych MEED CR233, 2022). Say so, and book it rather than examining by video.
If she competes under anti-doping rules, advise her to check any new medicine against UK Anti-Doping resources before starting it.

community.t: Beat (the UK eating-disorder charity) for information and helplines; a sports dietitian registered with the HCPC; sports and exercise medicine clinics; her club’s welfare officer if she chooses to involve them.

redFlags: Pain at rest or at night, or a fracture at a high-risk site (navicular, base of fifth metatarsal) — urgent orthopaedic or sports-medicine opinion
Signs of physical instability from restriction: fainting, palpitations, marked fatigue, rapid weight loss — same-day in-person assessment
Purging, laxative misuse or suicidal thoughts
psychosocial: What running means to her, training load, race calendar, coach and club pressures
Eating pattern, food rules, weight and shape worries, and how she copes with stress
ice: Idea: “It’s just bad luck with my foot”
Concern: losing fitness and losing running — “I don’t know who I am without it”
Expectation: a boot and a quick return to training

playbook.diagnosis: “Three stress fractures in a year isn’t bad luck. The commonest reason in runners is the body getting less fuel than the training uses, so it cuts back on periods, hormones and bone repair. That’s called relative energy deficiency in sport, and it’s very fixable.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of your body like a phone on low-power mode. When there isn’t enough charge, it switches off background apps to keep going — and periods and bone repair are the first apps it shuts down.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me running is everything to you. That’s exactly why I want to fix the cause, so you can keep running for years instead of breaking every few months.”
management.psychosocial: Work with her identity as an athlete: frame fuelling as performance, offer a sports dietitian first, keep the eating-disorder route open, and respect her wish to keep the club out of it.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face exam this week, foot imaging, relative rest from running
Pregnancy test, FBC, ferritin, U and E, bone profile, vitamin D, TFTs, coeliac serology, LH, FSH, oestradiol, prolactin; DXA
Refer to sports and exercise medicine and a sports dietitian; immediate eating-disorder referral if one is suspected (NICE NG69)
safetyNet: Severe or constant pain, fainting, palpitations or falling mood — contact the practice or 111 the same day
Review in person this week and again with results

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by doctors who treat the foot and miss the person. The marks sit in recognising the pattern, asking about food and periods without shaming her, and building a plan she will accept.

items.fail: Arranging an X-ray and a walking boot and discussing return to running, with no question about eating, periods or bone density.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Three fractures in a year needs a search for the cause (IOC REDs 2023, international; NICE NG69 on DXA with recurrent fractures).
items.fix: Say it out loud early: “Three in a year tells me something bigger is going on — can we look at why?”

items.fail: Accepting “isn’t that normal for runners?” about irregular periods, or not asking about the pill.
items.why: Amenorrhoea is the key clue; withdrawal bleeds on a combined pill hide it. Missing a pregnancy test in amenorrhoea is a safety error.
items.fix: Ask about periods and contraception directly, explain why, and do a pregnancy test before anything else.

items.fail: Leading with “Do you have an eating disorder?” or pushing for disclosure when she closes down.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s cues” and “appeared judgemental”. Shame shuts the conversation for good.
items.fix: Explain why you ask, normalise it, accept a partial answer, and leave the door open: “You don’t have to answer everything today.”

items.fail: Telling her she must stop running without exploring what running means to her.
items.why: Her hidden fear is losing her identity. A plan that ignores it will not be followed.
items.fix: Ask what stepping back would mean, then frame fuelling and rest as the way to keep running long term.

items.fail: “Examining” the foot and judging her physical state over video.
items.why: Unsafe assessment: fracture examination and physical-risk checks (MEED CR233, 2022) need an in-person review.
items.fix: Name the limit and book her in person this week, with observations and a weight.

items.fail: Leaving without a plan for bone density, the dietitian or the eating-disorder route.
items.why: “Management plan insufficiently developed.” The deficit that caused the fractures is still there.
items.fix: Give a clear list: in-person exam, bloods and DXA, sports medicine and dietitian, and the conditions for an eating-disorder referral.

items.fail: Sharing concerns with her coach or club “to help her”.
items.why: She is an adult with capacity; sharing without consent breaches GMC confidentiality guidance.
items.fix: Ask whether she wants anyone involved, and respect her answer.

wordPics.fail: Books an X-ray and a boot and discusses return to running; never asks about eating or periods; accepts “it’s normal for runners”; no DXA or bloods; or confronts her with “you have an eating disorder” and loses her.
wordPics.pass: Recognises recurrent fractures as a warning sign; asks about eating and periods including the pill; arranges exam, imaging, bloods and DXA; refers to sports medicine and a dietitian; safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains low energy availability in words she accepts; ties fuelling to her own goal of running well; does a pregnancy test first; keeps the eating-disorder door open without labelling; arranges in-person physical-risk checks; respects her confidentiality with the club.

avoid.dont: “Missing periods is normal when you run a lot.”
avoid.instead: “It’s common in runners, but it’s a sign your body is short of energy, and it weakens bone.”
avoid.why: Normalising amenorrhoea is the exact error this station tests.

avoid.dont: “I think you have anorexia and you need to stop running.”
avoid.instead: “Repeated fractures usually mean the body needs more fuel for the training. Can we look at that together?”
avoid.why: A label and a ban end the conversation; a shared explanation keeps her engaged.

avoid.dont: “Let’s get you a boot and you can build back up in six weeks.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll look after the foot, and I also want to find out why this is the third one.”
avoid.why: Treating only the bone guarantees a fourth fracture.

avoid.instead: “Repeated fractures usually mean the body needs more fuel for the training. Can we look at that together?”
avoid.why: A label and a ban end the conversation; a shared explanation keeps her engaged.

avoid.dont: “Let’s get you a boot and you can build back up in six weeks.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll look after the foot, and I also want to find out why this is the third one.”
avoid.why: Treating only the bone guarantees a fourth fracture.

SCA_MODELS.text: Hi Orla, I’m Dr Lee. I’ve seen the walk-in note about your foot. I’m sorry — I can hear how frustrating this is. Tell me what’s happened, and what you’re hoping we can do today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Opens with her story and her expectations, not a checklist

SCA_MODELS.text: It’s my foot again. They think it’s another stress fracture — third one this year. I’ve got races coming up, so I just need it sorted. A boot or whatever, so I can get back to training fast.

Getting you back running is exactly what I want too. I’ll make sure the foot is properly looked after. But I’d also like to understand why this keeps happening, because three in a year tells me something. Can we cover both today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Agrees a shared agenda that includes the systemic question

SCA_MODELS.text: I suppose. I just thought it was bad luck.
Talk me through the foot first — where is the pain, and is it there when you walk, or only when you run?
SCA_MODELS.why: Focused fracture history to judge severity and site

SCA_MODELS.text: It hurts walking now. It started as just a niggle on long runs and I kept going.
Thanks. And what does a normal week of training look like at the moment — has anything changed in the last few months?
SCA_MODELS.why: Establishes training load, the other half of the energy balance

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ve been building my mileage for the season. I train most days.

That’s a big load. Repeated stress fractures in runners often come down to the body not getting enough fuel for the training — often without anyone meaning it to. Could you walk me through what you’d eat on a typical training day?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why before asking a sensitive question, so it lands as curiosity not accusation

SCA_MODELS.text: I eat healthily. I’m careful, that’s all — you have to be at my level.

Lots of athletes say that. Can I ask a bit more — do you ever skip meals, have rules about what you will or won’t eat, or feel guilty if you eat more than planned? Any making yourself sick or using laxatives? There’s no judgement here; I ask everyone who has bones breaking like this.
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens restriction, food rules and compensatory behaviours in a normalised way

SCA_MODELS.text: I don’t really want to get into all that. I’m not ill. I just watch what I eat.
That’s fair, and you don’t have to answer everything today. I’ll leave the door open. Can I ask about your periods — are they regular, and are you on any contraception?
SCA_MODELS.why: Respects her pace and moves to the key clue: menstrual history and the pill

SCA_MODELS.text: I don’t really keep track. Isn’t that normal for runners anyway?

It’s common, but it isn’t normal or harmless — it’s one of the clearest signs the body is running low on energy, and it weakens bone. And if someone is on the combined pill, the monthly bleed can hide the problem completely, so I’ll check exactly what you take.
SCA_MODELS.why: Corrects the myth and names the masking effect of the pill

SCA_MODELS.text: How are you in yourself — energy, mood, sleep, picking up lots of colds, or feeling your running has stalled even though you train harder?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens the wider effects of low energy availability

SCA_MODELS.text: I’m tired, but everyone’s tired. I do get stressed about races.
You’ve said a few times you don’t want to lose fitness. What would it mean for you if you had to step back from running for a while?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores the real concern behind “just sort my foot”

SCA_MODELS.text: Running is basically everything. If I can’t train I don’t really know who I am. That’s what scares me.
Thank you for telling me that. It makes complete sense that this feels threatening. My aim is the opposite of taking running away — it’s to stop your body breaking so you can keep doing it for years.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates the fear and reframes the doctor as an ally for her sport

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s what I think is going on. When training uses more energy than food puts back in, the body saves energy by turning down things it sees as optional — periods, hormones, bone repair. That’s called low energy availability, and it’s the commonest reason for repeated stress fractures in runners. It isn’t about willpower or blame.
SCA_MODELS.why: Plain-language explanation of REDs linking fractures, periods and fuel

SCA_MODELS.text: So you think I’m not eating enough?
I think it’s the most likely explanation, and I’d like to check rather than guess. The upside is real: athletes who fuel properly usually get their periods back, heal better and often run faster.
SCA_MODELS.why: Frames fuelling as the route to performance, not a punishment

SCA_MODELS.text: I hadn’t thought of it like that.

For the foot: I’d like to see you in person this week to examine it, check your weight, pulse and blood pressure, and arrange the right scan. Until then, please don’t run on it. If it’s in certain higher-risk spots in the foot, it needs a bone specialist quickly.
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges face-to-face assessment, imaging and relative rest; flags high-risk sites

SCA_MODELS.text: No running at all? Okay… if it means it heals properly.

Alongside that, some blood tests — a pregnancy test because periods are irregular, blood count, iron, vitamin D, kidney and bone salts, thyroid, coeliac and hormone levels — and a bone-density scan, because three fractures is enough reason to look.
SCA_MODELS.why: Pregnancy test first, then a targeted work-up and DXA

SCA_MODELS.text: Then I’d like to get you the right team: a sports medicine doctor and a sports dietitian who works with runners. And if food ever feels harder to manage than you’d like, there’s specialist support for that too — your choice when. How does that sound?
SCA_MODELS.why: Multidisciplinary referral offered as a choice, keeping the eating-disorder route open without labelling

SCA_MODELS.text: A dietitian’s fine. The other bit… maybe. Not yet.

That’s okay. If what we find suggests an eating problem, I’ll talk to you openly before referring, because early help works best. And one question for your club or coach — would you like me to share anything with them? Only if you want me to.
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest about the referral threshold; respects adult confidentiality

SCA_MODELS.text: No, keep it between us for now.

Of course. Please call us or 111 sooner if the pain becomes severe or constant at rest, you feel faint or dizzy, your heart races or feels irregular, or you notice your mood dropping badly. I’ll see you face to face this week and again when the results are back.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net, including physical-risk and mood symptoms, with booked follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That’s more than I expected, but it makes sense.
Can you tell me in your own words what we’re doing next, so I know I’ve explained it well?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back checks understanding

SCA_MODELS.text: Rest the foot, come in this week, bloods and a bone scan, see a sports doctor and dietitian. And think about the fuelling thing.
Perfect. You did the right thing getting this looked at properly. Anything else you wanted to ask?
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes warmly and shares the floor

SCA_STEM.name: Orla Devine
pmh: Two stress fractures in the past 12 months
meds: Current medication and contraception not recorded on the summary
SCA_STEM.recent: Walk-in centre attendance this week: suspected stress fracture of the foot, advised to see her GP. This would be her third stress fracture in a year. No bone-density scan or bone bloods on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation booked: “My foot again — I need it sorted so I can keep training.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: IOC consensus statement on REDs 2023 (international) · NICE NG69 (eating disorders, 2017, updated 2020) · RCPsych MEED CR233 (2022)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Three stress fractures in a year in a young woman who runs is a systemic warning, not bad luck. Screen for low energy availability, disordered eating and menstrual disturbance, look for low bone density, and treat the cause with a team, not just the bone.

points.h: Recurrent bone stress injury is the red flag
points.t: One stress fracture can follow a jump in training load. Repeated ones point to low energy availability and poor bone health. Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) is wider than the old female athlete triad: it affects men too, and reaches bone, hormones, mood, immunity, heart and performance [1].

points.h: Screen eating by conversation, not a score
points.t: Ask about intake against training, restriction, food rules, weight and shape worries, purging, laxatives and over-exercise. A tool such as SCOFF can prompt the conversation but must not be the only way you decide whether an eating disorder is present [2]. If you suspect one, refer immediately to the community eating-disorder service [2].

points.h: Periods are a vital sign, and the pill can hide them
points.t: Absent or infrequent periods in an athlete are a sign of low energy availability, not a normal effect of running. Withdrawal bleeds on a combined pill mask this, so ask what she takes. Always do a pregnancy test first in amenorrhoea, then LH, FSH, oestradiol, prolactin and TFTs.

points.h: Investigate the bone and the cause
points.t: Confirm the fracture (MRI is the most sensitive test; X-ray is often normal early). Bloods: FBC, ferritin, U and E, bone profile, vitamin D, TFTs, coeliac serology. Consider DXA: NICE NG69 advises DXA earlier than usual when there are recurrent fractures [2]. A fracture at a high-risk site (for example the navicular or the base of the fifth metatarsal) needs an urgent orthopaedic or sports-medicine opinion.

points.h: Check physical risk before assuming she is well
points.t: If eating is significantly restricted, assess medical risk in person: weight and BMI, lying and standing pulse and BP, temperature, the sit-up–squat–stand test and an ECG and electrolytes if indicated [3]. A video call cannot do this.

points.h: Treat the energy deficit, not the fracture alone
points.t: Relative rest from impact, more fuel, and a team: sports and exercise medicine, a sports dietitian, and eating-disorder or psychology input where needed. Correct vitamin D deficiency (dose per BNF). The combined pill is not advised to protect bone in hypothalamic amenorrhoea; if hormone therapy is needed, specialists use transdermal oestradiol with cyclical progesterone [1].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; lets her explain the foot and her goal of racing; agrees an agenda that includes “why does this keep happening?”.
Training load, identity as a runner, club or coach pressure, stress about races, mood and sleep.
Picks up “I’m careful what I eat”, “isn’t that normal for runners?” and the fear of losing fitness, and explores each.
Idea: bad luck; concern: losing running and the identity attached to it; expectation: a quick fix to keep training.
Face-to-face exam with weight, pulse, BP, temperature; imaging of the foot; pregnancy test, FBC, ferritin, U and E, bone profile, vitamin D, TFTs, coeliac, LH, FSH, oestradiol, prolactin; DXA.
Low energy availability (REDs) versus training error alone; disordered eating; other causes of amenorrhoea (pregnancy, thyroid, prolactin, PCOS); coeliac or vitamin D deficiency.
High-risk fracture site; physical instability from restriction (bradycardia, postural drop, electrolyte disturbance); a significant eating disorder needing immediate referral.
Recurrent bone stress injury, probably from relative energy deficiency in sport, shared in plain language without blame.
Relative rest from impact; team referral (sports medicine, sports dietitian, eating-disorder service if suspected); fuelling framed as the route to performance.
Checks contraception (pill can mask amenorrhoea, and does not protect bone); vitamin D replacement if low; mood and stress.
Face-to-face review this week, results review, named red flags (fainting, palpitations, severe pain, low mood), confidentiality with her club respected.

social.t: For a competitive athlete, running can be her identity, social world and coping strategy. Leanness culture, coach expectations and race targets can drive under-fuelling; explore them without blame.
“Clean” or “careful” eating in athletes can hide restriction. Many do not see it as a problem, so aim for trust and a door left open rather than a confession today.

legal.t: She is a competent adult. Do not share information with her coach, club or governing body without her consent (GMC Confidentiality, 2017), unless there is a serious risk to life.

legal.h: Capacity and the Mental Health Act
legal.t: Her decisions about training and treatment are hers while she has capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Compulsory treatment only arises in severe, life-threatening eating disorders and is not the issue today.

professional.t: Fracture assessment and eating-disorder physical-risk checks need an in-person review (RCPsych MEED CR233, 2022). Say so, and book it rather than examining by video.
If she competes under anti-doping rules, advise her to check any new medicine against UK Anti-Doping resources before starting it.

community.t: Beat (the UK eating-disorder charity) for information and helplines; a sports dietitian registered with the HCPC; sports and exercise medicine clinics; her club’s welfare officer if she chooses to involve them.

redFlags: Pain at rest or at night, or a fracture at a high-risk site (navicular, base of fifth metatarsal) — urgent orthopaedic or sports-medicine opinion
Signs of physical instability from restriction: fainting, palpitations, marked fatigue, rapid weight loss — same-day in-person assessment
Purging, laxative misuse or suicidal thoughts
psychosocial: What running means to her, training load, race calendar, coach and club pressures
Eating pattern, food rules, weight and shape worries, and how she copes with stress
ice: Idea: “It’s just bad luck with my foot”
Concern: losing fitness and losing running — “I don’t know who I am without it”
Expectation: a boot and a quick return to training

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Three stress fractures in a year isn’t bad luck. The commonest reason in runners is the body getting less fuel than the training uses, so it cuts back on periods, hormones and bone repair. That’s called relative energy deficiency in sport, and it’s very fixable.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of your body like a phone on low-power mode. When there isn’t enough charge, it switches off background apps to keep going — and periods and bone repair are the first apps it shuts down.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me running is everything to you. That’s exactly why I want to fix the cause, so you can keep running for years instead of breaking every few months.”
management.psychosocial: Work with her identity as an athlete: frame fuelling as performance, offer a sports dietitian first, keep the eating-disorder route open, and respect her wish to keep the club out of it.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face exam this week, foot imaging, relative rest from running
Pregnancy test, FBC, ferritin, U and E, bone profile, vitamin D, TFTs, coeliac serology, LH, FSH, oestradiol, prolactin; DXA
Refer to sports and exercise medicine and a sports dietitian; immediate eating-disorder referral if one is suspected (NICE NG69)
safetyNet: Severe or constant pain, fainting, palpitations or falling mood — contact the practice or 111 the same day
Review in person this week and again with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by doctors who treat the foot and miss the person. The marks sit in recognising the pattern, asking about food and periods without shaming her, and building a plan she will accept.

items.fail: Arranging an X-ray and a walking boot and discussing return to running, with no question about eating, periods or bone density.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Three fractures in a year needs a search for the cause (IOC REDs 2023, international; NICE NG69 on DXA with recurrent fractures).
items.fix: Say it out loud early: “Three in a year tells me something bigger is going on — can we look at why?”

items.fail: Accepting “isn’t that normal for runners?” about irregular periods, or not asking about the pill.
items.why: Amenorrhoea is the key clue; withdrawal bleeds on a combined pill hide it. Missing a pregnancy test in amenorrhoea is a safety error.
items.fix: Ask about periods and contraception directly, explain why, and do a pregnancy test before anything else.

items.fail: Leading with “Do you have an eating disorder?” or pushing for disclosure when she closes down.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s cues” and “appeared judgemental”. Shame shuts the conversation for good.
items.fix: Explain why you ask, normalise it, accept a partial answer, and leave the door open: “You don’t have to answer everything today.”

items.fail: Telling her she must stop running without exploring what running means to her.
items.why: Her hidden fear is losing her identity. A plan that ignores it will not be followed.
items.fix: Ask what stepping back would mean, then frame fuelling and rest as the way to keep running long term.

items.fail: “Examining” the foot and judging her physical state over video.
items.why: Unsafe assessment: fracture examination and physical-risk checks (MEED CR233, 2022) need an in-person review.
items.fix: Name the limit and book her in person this week, with observations and a weight.

items.fail: Leaving without a plan for bone density, the dietitian or the eating-disorder route.
items.why: “Management plan insufficiently developed.” The deficit that caused the fractures is still there.
items.fix: Give a clear list: in-person exam, bloods and DXA, sports medicine and dietitian, and the conditions for an eating-disorder referral.

items.fail: Sharing concerns with her coach or club “to help her”.
items.why: She is an adult with capacity; sharing without consent breaches GMC confidentiality guidance.
items.fix: Ask whether she wants anyone involved, and respect her answer.
